idiom_name: grantor + attorney (private forwarding members) + requestor, with the grant declared by friendship or the language's nearest equivalent
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: the grantor keeps its implementation private and befriends exactly one gatekeeper type; the gatekeeper's own interface is private too, it forwards only a cohesive subset of the grantor's private operations (each forwarding member is one delegating call, classically static and inline, taking the grantor by reference), and it declares which collaborators may use it. The grantor therefore has one friend instead of many, the requestor's dependency is limited to the forwarded subset, and the remaining private members are free to change. Where the language has restricted-visibility syntax (module paths, file scope, qualified packages) prefer that, and keep the hand-built attorney for grants that must name a collaborator. Every realization is source-level: state plainly that this is encapsulation against accident, not a runtime security control. Note: constrained friend declarations (friend void f() requires C<T>) with requires clauses have known compiler bugs in Clang (llvm/llvm-project#58859, #145505) where access checking fails incorrectly; prefer unconstrained friend templates when private access is needed.
pitfalls: Making the attorney's members public (or befriending more than the intended requestor) turns a narrow gate into a general access path to the grantor's internals.
Forwarding every private member instead of a cohesive subset reproduces friendship with extra steps: the attorney now has to be updated by every change in the grantor and protects nothing.
Treating the grant as protection against untrusted code: it is a compiler-checked source-level structure, and reflection, macro tricks or binary patching ignore it.

Constrained friend templates with requires clauses trigger access-control bugs in Clang (llvm/llvm-project#58859, #145505) where the compiler incorrectly forgets the friendship during constraint checking. Use unconstrained friend templates when the attorney needs private access.

Silent signature drift: a forwarding member that accepts a type convertible to the private parameter (int vs double, or a default argument) compiles but forwards a different call than intended. Keep forwarding signatures identical to the private signatures.
Attorneys that outlive the grantor: if the attorney is a free class distributed separately, it cannot be shipped without the class that declared it a friend, creating a distribution coupling.

Wrong move: publish a private nested type through a broadly included attorney header; failure: every includer can name that type and call all of its public members, so the friend list no longer controls use; instead: keep the alias header-scoped to the requestor or expose only private forwarding functions.

Wrong move: return std::list<T>::iterator or alias the hidden container to make traversal easy; failure: representation, node type and invalidation guarantees become client dependencies; instead: return a stable nested view/iterator contract and mediate its construction through the attorney.

Wrong move: use the attorney to solve ABI or compile-time dependency churn; failure: a public alias to the implementation type still requires its definition and couples headers; instead: use pImpl for the compilation firewall and add a narrow attorney only in the privileged component's boundary.

Wrong move: require user types to expose their extension hook (iterator core operations, serialize()) publicly so your library can call it; failure: every user's public API is polluted by the extension protocol and unrelated callers can bypass the facade; instead: ship one library-owned gateway type as Boost does (boost::iterator_core_access, boost::serialization::access) that user types declare friend, keeping the hooks private.

Wrong move: ship the attorney with public static forwarders marked 'for internal use only'; failure: every consumer of the public header can call them, so the restriction is a comment rather than a boundary (Sparta's TreeNodePrivateAttorney must warn users away by documentation alone); instead: keep the forwarders private, friend the intended requestors, and place the attorney in an internal header outside the public include path as fsfw does.

Wrong move: leave friend or attorney declarations that end up touching no private names; failure: the empirical study of open-source C++ (Márton and Porkoláb 2018) found many friend declarations access only public members, so the grant hides a coupling and misleads reviewers about what is privileged; instead: audit every grant and delete declarations whose forwarders could be replaced by public calls.
